explanations.explanation: Egypt it is. The LORD says, “Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in the land where I tell you.” (Gen 26:2) So Isaac gets a no and a yes in one breath. That's about as clear as directions get, and I've followed worse ones off a recipe card.
Moab never comes up in this passage, friend. The LORD says, “Do not go down to Egypt.” (Gen 26:2) That's the one place He names. Isaac is to settle where God tells him.

Assyria isn't in this scene at all. The LORD names Egypt: “Do not go down to Egypt.” (Gen 26:2) Then He says to settle in the land where He tells Isaac. One no, one yes, nothing more complicated than that.

Lands, yes. The LORD says, “For I will give all these lands to you and your offspring…” (Gen 26:3) That promise comes right alongside “…I will be with you and bless you.” Isaac gets a whole lot more than a spot to put his tent.
Herds do show up later, since Isaac ends up with plenty of them. But that isn't what God promises here. He says, “…I will give all these lands to you and your offspring…” (Gen 26:3)

Treasures sounds nice, I'll give you that. But the LORD doesn't say it here. What He says is, “…I will give all these lands to you and your offspring…” (Gen 26:3) Lands first, and He's with Isaac the whole way.

True. God says, “…through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed…” (Gen 26:4) He says it to Isaac right when there's a famine in the land (Gen 26:1). Isaac is one man, and God is talking about all nations. That's a big promise, friend.

This one is true, friend. God tells Isaac, “…through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed…” (Gen 26:4) It sits right beside the promise about descendants like the stars. The blessing is meant to reach well past Isaac's own tent.

Right. God says it's “…because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws.” (Gen 26:5) Abraham, Isaac's father, listened and kept what God gave him. The text puts it just that plainly.

Forty days of fasting isn't mentioned here. God's reason is that “…Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws.” (Gen 26:5) Listening and keeping, that's what the text points to.

Giving away his wealth isn't the reason God gives. He says, “…Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws.” (Gen 26:5) Abraham, Isaac's father, is remembered here for listening.

Sister. “She is my sister.” Isaac says, when the men of that place ask about his wife, Rebekah. (Gen 26:7) That's a tricky answer to give about the woman you married. The text says he was afraid to say, “She is my wife…”
Servant isn't what he says. Isaac tells the men, “She is my sister.” (Gen 26:7) Rebekah is his wife, and he was afraid to say so.
Daughter would be a stretch, friend, and it isn't what Isaac says. He tells the men of Gerar, “She is my sister.” (Gen 26:7) Rebekah is really his wife.

explanations.answer: He's afraid they'll kill him for her
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says he was afraid to say, “She is my wife…” since he thought, “The men of this place will kill me on account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful.” (Gen 26:7) Isaac's fear is doing the talking here. I've said some silly things when I was scared too.

explanations.answer: He hopes the king will give him land
explanations.explanation: Land from the king isn't the reason. The text says Isaac was afraid, and he thought, “The men of this place will kill me on account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful.” (Gen 26:7) Nobody in this verse is working a land deal. It's fear doing the talking.

explanations.answer: He wants the men of Gerar to trust him
explanations.explanation: Trust sounds like a nice reason, but it isn't the one in the text. Isaac was afraid, and he thought, “The men of this place will kill me on account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful.” (Gen 26:7) I think a man who's scared for his life isn't thinking about winning anybody's trust. He's just trying to get through the day, and that sister line came out of a scared place.

That's it. Abimelech “…was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah.” (Gen 26:8) That look from the window shows him who Rebekah is to Isaac, and he sends for Isaac and says, “So she is really your wife!” (Gen 26:9) Isaac's story just got caught by a window.
Sheep counting isn't what he sees. The text says Abimelech “…was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah.” (Gen 26:8) Nobody counts anything in this verse.
Weaving isn't in this scene at all. Abimelech “…was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah.” (Gen 26:8) That one look from the window is what gives it away.

Guilt. Abimelech says, “One of the people could easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us.” (Gen 26:10) I think he's rattled by what could have happened. Isaac had said she was his sister, and the king did NOT take that lightly.
War isn't the word Abimelech uses. He says, “…you would have brought guilt upon us.” (Gen 26:10) Guilt is what he's worried about.
Drought would be a rough follow-up to a famine, but that isn't what he says. Abimelech tells Isaac, “…you would have brought guilt upon us.” (Gen 26:10) The worry is guilt for his people.

True. Abimelech warns all the people, “Whoever harms this man or his wife will surely be put to death.” (Gen 26:11) Isaac was afraid of being killed, and now the king himself has said no one touches him or Rebekah. That's a pretty big turn.
This one is true, friend. Abimelech warns all the people, “Whoever harms this man or his wife will surely be put to death.” (Gen 26:11) He says it to everyone, so Isaac and Rebekah are covered.
Yes. The text says “…he became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy.” (Gen 26:13) That comes right after the LORD blessed him. Isaac keeps going up and up.
Running out is the opposite of what happens. The text says “…he became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy.” (Gen 26:13) The LORD blessed him, and it shows.

explanations.answer: He gives it all to the king
explanations.explanation: Handing it all to the king isn't what happens. The LORD blessed Isaac, and then “…he became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy.” (Gen 26:13) Nobody's passing him a collection plate. The verse only goes one way, and that's up. I wish my cookie jar worked like that.

Not quite, friend. The text says he owned so many flocks, herds and servants “…that the Philistines envied him.” (Gen 26:14) Envied and thrilled are two different things. And the very next verse has the wells stopped up with dirt.

False is right. The text says Isaac owned so many flocks, herds and servants “…that the Philistines envied him.” (Gen 26:14) Envy is a long way from being happy for someone. And you can see where it leads in the next verse.

Yes. “…the Philistines took dirt and stopped up all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.” (Gen 26:15) Those wells went back to Abraham, Isaac's father. Dirt was the tool, and it was all of the wells. That's a LOT of shoveling, and I've done my share of digging out of a drawer, so I respect the effort.
Poison isn't in the text. It says the Philistines “…took dirt and stopped up all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.” (Gen 26:15) Dirt, not poison.

No guards here. The text says the Philistines “…took dirt and stopped up all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.” (Gen 26:15) They filled the wells instead of watching them.
True. Abimelech tells Isaac, “Depart from us, for you are much too powerful for us.” (Gen 26:16) That's the king talking, the same king who said no one should touch Isaac. Now he wants Isaac gone.
This one is true, friend. Abimelech says, “Depart from us, for you are much too powerful for us.” (Gen 26:16) That's right after the envy and the plugged wells. Isaac is asked to leave.

Not this time. The text says Isaac “…gave these wells the same names his father had given them.” (Gen 26:18) He doesn't rename them. He keeps the names Abraham chose, and I think that says something sweet about Isaac.
False is right. Isaac “…gave these wells the same names his father had given them.” (Gen 26:18) Same wells, same names. Abraham's names stay.

Yes, the herdsmen of Gerar. Isaac's servants had found a well of fresh water in the valley (Gen 26:19). Then Gerar's herdsmen quarrel with Isaac's herdsmen and say, “The water is ours!” (Gen 26:20) Isaac named the well Esek, because they contended with him. Somebody found water and somebody else filed a claim. I've seen that kind of thing over a parking spot.

Lot's herdsmen aren't in this chapter. The ones who quarrel with Isaac's herdsmen are the herdsmen of Gerar, and they say, “The water is ours!” (Gen 26:20) So the claim comes from Gerar's side of the valley.

Midian's shepherds don't show up here. The text has the herdsmen of Gerar quarreling with Isaac's herdsmen, and they say, “The water is ours!” (Gen 26:20) Gerar is the place where Isaac had been settled (Gen 26:17). So it's the neighbors making the claim.
Not quite, friend. The text says “…they dug another well and quarreled over that one also; so he named it Sitnah.” (Gen 26:21) A second dig, and a second argument. Isaac keeps going anyway.
False is right. The text says they “…dug another well and quarreled over that one also; so he named it Sitnah.” (Gen 26:21) Two wells, two quarrels. Peace comes at the next one.

Yes. Isaac names the well Rehoboth and says, “At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.” (Gen 26:22) After two quarrels, nobody fights over this one. I think you can hear the relief.
A city isn't what Isaac says. He says, “At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.” (Gen 26:22) Room is the word.
The famine isn't what Isaac mentions here. He says, “At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.” (Gen 26:22) The well is about room, not the famine.
Yes. The LORD says, “Do not be afraid, for I am with you.” (Gen 26:24) He gives Isaac the command and the reason in one line. That's a good one to hang on a kitchen wall.
Leaving isn't mentioned. The LORD says, “Do not be afraid, for I am with you.” (Gen 26:24) And Isaac pitches his tent there right after.
God doesn't say anything about digging. His words are, “Do not be afraid, for I am with you.” (Gen 26:24) Isaac's servants do dig a well there, but that's after.

Multiply. The LORD says, “I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of My servant Abraham.” (Gen 26:24) It's Isaac's blessing, and Abraham's name is in it too. More descendants, as promised.

Protect sounds like a nice promise, but it isn't the word here. The LORD says, “I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of My servant Abraham.” (Gen 26:24) Bless and multiply are the promises on the table. Stick with the word God used, baker.

Gather is what I do with crumbs at the end of a batch, but it isn't the word here. The LORD says, “I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of My servant Abraham.” (Gen 26:24) Multiply is what He promises. Bigger family, not a tidier one.

An altar, yes. “So Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD…” (Gen 26:25) The LORD appears to him that night in verse 24, and the altar comes in verse 25. After that Isaac pitches his tent, and his servants dig a well.

No tower here, friend. The text says, “…Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD…” (Gen 26:25) There are no blueprints for a tower anywhere in this verse. Just an altar and a man calling on the LORD.

A storehouse isn't in the text. Isaac “…built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD…” (Gen 26:25) He was exceedingly wealthy back in verse 13, so a storehouse wouldn't be a crazy guess. But the verse gives an altar.

explanations.answer: Hated him and sent him away
explanations.explanation: Yes. Isaac asks, “You hated me and sent me away.” (Gen 26:27) He doesn't wait around to say it. I think that line has some sting to it.
Nope, Isaac isn't talking about his flocks and herds. He says, “You hated me and sent me away.” (Gen 26:27) That's about how they treated him, not what they took. Short and it lands.

explanations.answer: Mocked his God and his altar
explanations.explanation: Mocking isn't what Isaac says. He first asks, “Why have you come to me?” and then tells them, “You hated me and sent me away.” (Gen 26:27) Nothing about his God or his altar comes up in those words. Hated and sent away is the whole charge, and I think it carries plenty of sting by itself.

explanations.answer: An oath that he won't harm them
explanations.explanation: That's what they ask. They say, “We recommend that there should now be an oath between us and you.” Then they add, “…that you will not harm us, just as we have not harmed you…” (Gen 26:28-29) They say they can plainly see the LORD has been with Isaac.

explanations.answer: A share of all his new wells
explanations.explanation: No share of wells is asked for. They ask for a covenant “…that you will not harm us, just as we have not harmed you…” (Gen 26:29) It's an oath they want.

explanations.answer: His servants to fight their wars
explanations.explanation: Fighting isn't what they ask for. They say, “Let us make a covenant with you that you will not harm us, just as we have not harmed you…” (Gen 26:28-29) They want an oath of peace.

True. “On that same day, Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug.” (Gen 26:32) They tell him, “We have found water!” Isaac's guests had just left him in peace (Gen 26:31). Peace and water in one day is a good day, friend.
This one is true, friend. The text says on that same day, Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug. They say, “We have found water!” (Gen 26:32)
Grief. The text says, “…they brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.” (Gen 26:35) Esau, Isaac's son, married Judith and Basemath at forty. It's a quiet, heavy note at the end of the chapter.
Honor isn't what the text says. It says Judith and Basemath “…brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.” (Gen 26:35) That's a heavy line to end the chapter on.
Wealth isn't in this verse. The text says they “…brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.” (Gen 26:35) These are the wives of Esau, Isaac's son.
